title: The truck that wasn't there

beats.say: A hundred million dollars of AI freight, stolen. Mostly with paperwork.
Why chase a truck full of servers? One AI server rack costs about three million dollars. That truck is a vault on wheels.
In one big theft, the thieves spoofed the GPS, feeding the tracker a fake location. The dashboard showed a truck that wasn't there.
But that was the exception. Overhaul says ninety-two percent of high-value tech thefts used deception, not force.
So how do you trick your way into a truck? Through freight brokers, a marriage bureau for cargo and truckers.
The thieves break into a broker's account and post shipments that don't exist. Real truckers bid, and take the bait.
Then trucking companies get a link. One click, and the thieves own that account too, bidding under a real name.
Imagine mummy's WhatsApp is hijacked: give dad's suits to my friend. The dhobi isn't dumb. The account looked right.
So who drives away? Sometimes a real driver, hired without knowing. Sometimes an accomplice with a fake licence.
Force did show up, twice. Thieves rammed the security escorts, and the drivers just kept going.
Even then, Scott Cornell of SPG Cargo traced both to one gap: those drivers weren't properly vetted.
So the weak spot was never the truck. It was trust.
Cornell wants proper driver checks and digital bills of lading, because paper ones let thieves rewrite what's in the box.
If a login can be borrowed this easily, what else do we trust just because the account looks right?

breaking.say: Breaking: a hundred million dollars of AI freight, stolen. Mostly with paperwork.

teaser.say: Today: the truck that wasn't there. Why it matters: your logins work the same way.

greeting.say: Good morning, it's the twenty-eighth, and this is The Daily Habit.

talk.say: So the weak spot was never the truck. It was trust. And trust, it turns out, can be borrowed with one click.
